units.title: Our Country's Symbols
units.blurb: The flag, the bald eagle, the Liberty Bell, the Statue of Liberty, our national anthem and the buildings of Washington, D.C.: what each one stands for.

units.title: Rules, Leaders and Helpers
units.blurb: Why we have rules, who makes them at home, at school and in town, the people who help our community, and how we choose leaders by voting.

units.title: Holidays and Why We Have Them
units.blurb: The national holidays we keep through the year, what each one remembers, and how families mark them.

units.title: The First Americans
units.blurb: The many Native nations who lived here long before Europeans came, their homes and foods, and Native nations today.

units.title: Explorers and Early Colonies
units.blurb: Explorers who crossed the ocean, the first English settlements at Jamestown and Plymouth, the 1621 harvest feast, and the thirteen colonies.

units.title: The Revolution and a New Nation
units.blurb: Why the colonists broke away, the Declaration of Independence, George Washington, the heroes of the Revolution, and the Constitution as the country's rulebook.

units.title: A Growing and Changing Country
units.blurb: Lewis and Clark and the pioneers, Abraham Lincoln and the end of slavery, heroes of freedom, inventors, and fifty states.

units.title: Heroes of Service
units.blurb: People who served others and worked for fairness: nurses and soldiers, Rosa Parks and Dr. King, astronauts who reached the Moon, and how you can help, too.

topics.title: The American Flag
topics.short: Our flag has 13 stripes for the first 13 colonies and 50 stars for the 50 states today.
topics.trouble: Children mix up the two numbers: they think the stripes stand for states, or that there is one stripe for each state. The stripes are for the 13 colonies that became the first states; the stars are for the 50 states now.

topics.title: The Bald Eagle
topics.short: The bald eagle, a big bird of North America, has been on the Great Seal of the United States since 1782 and stands for strength and freedom; in 2024 Congress made it the official national bird.
topics.trouble: "Bald" makes children think the eagle has no feathers on its head. Its head is covered with white feathers; long ago "bald" also meant "white-headed."

topics.title: The Liberty Bell
topics.short: The Liberty Bell in Philadelphia is a symbol of freedom; it has a famous crack and its words say to proclaim liberty throughout the land.
topics.trouble: Children think the Liberty Bell is still rung like a church bell. Because of its crack it has been silent for over 150 years; it is kept where visitors can see it.

topics.title: The Statue of Liberty
topics.short: The Statue of Liberty, a gift from the people of France in 1886, holds up a torch in New York Harbor to welcome people arriving by sea.
topics.trouble: Children are surprised the statue is green and think it was painted. It is made of copper, which was shiny brown at first and turned green over many years in the weather.

topics.title: Our National Anthem
topics.short: Francis Scott Key wrote "The Star-Spangled Banner" in 1814 after he saw the flag still flying over Fort McHenry after a long battle.
topics.trouble: Children think the anthem was always our national song. Key wrote the words as a poem in 1814; Congress made it the national anthem much later, in 1931.

topics.title: Our Capital, Washington, D.C.
topics.short: Washington, D.C., is our nation's capital: Congress meets in the Capitol, the President lives and works in the White House, and monuments honor great Americans.
topics.trouble: Children confuse Washington, D.C., with the state of Washington, and the Capitol with the White House. The city is on the East Coast, far from the state; Congress works in the Capitol, the President in the White House.

topics.title: Why We Have Rules
topics.short: Rules keep us safe, help us be fair and help us get along, at home, at school and at play.
topics.trouble: Children see rules only as a way to get in trouble. Ask what would happen without the rule (no taking turns, no stopping at the crosswalk); rules protect everyone, including them.

topics.title: Rules and Laws
topics.short: A law is a rule for everyone in a town, state or country, made by leaders the people choose; laws apply to grown-ups too.
topics.trouble: Children think laws are only for children, or that grown-ups and leaders do not have to follow them. Laws apply to everyone, even the President.

topics.title: Community Helpers
topics.short: Firefighters, police officers, doctors and nurses, teachers, mail carriers and many others help our community, and each has a special job.
topics.trouble: Children match each helper to only one tool or uniform and miss what the helper does. Ask "What does this helper do for us?" not only "What does this helper wear?"

topics.title: Leaders and Voting
topics.short: In a vote, each person gets one choice and the choice with the most votes wins; Americans vote to choose leaders like a mayor, a governor and the President.
topics.trouble: Children count who shouts loudest or which choice they like as the winner. A vote is fair because every vote counts the same, and we count them all.

topics.title: Being a Good Citizen
topics.short: A good citizen follows the rules, tells the truth, helps others, takes care of shared places and, as a grown-up, votes.
topics.trouble: Children think "citizen" means only grown-ups or only famous people. Anyone can practice good citizenship by helping, sharing and caring for their community.

topics.title: Independence Day
topics.short: On July 4 we celebrate the birthday of our country: on July 4, 1776, leaders adopted the Declaration of Independence.
topics.trouble: Children think the Fourth of July is about fireworks or the end of a war. It remembers the day in 1776 when the Declaration of Independence was adopted; the war went on for years after.

topics.title: Thanksgiving Day
topics.short: On the fourth Thursday of November, families give thanks; it remembers the harvest feast of 1621 shared by the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people.
topics.trouble: Children think the Pilgrims held a Thanksgiving every year from 1621 on. The 1621 feast was a harvest celebration; President Lincoln made Thanksgiving a national holiday in 1863.

topics.title: Washington's Birthday (Presidents' Day)
topics.short: On the third Monday of February we honor George Washington, the first President, and many people honor all the Presidents.
topics.trouble: Children think the holiday falls on Washington's real birthday. Washington was born on February 22, 1732; the holiday moved to the third Monday of February in 1971, so it never lands on the 22nd.

topics.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Day
topics.short: On the third Monday of January we honor Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., who led peaceful marches and speeches so that all people would be treated fairly.
topics.trouble: Children think Dr. King worked alone or long ago in the time of Lincoln. He was one of many people in the civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s, about a hundred years after Lincoln.

topics.title: Memorial Day and Veterans Day
topics.short: Memorial Day (the last Monday of May) remembers service members who died for our country; Veterans Day (November 11) thanks everyone who has served.
topics.trouble: Children mix up the two days. Memorial Day remembers those who died in service; Veterans Day thanks all who served, living or not.

topics.title: Juneteenth, Labor Day and Other Holidays
topics.short: Juneteenth (June 19) remembers the end of slavery in Texas in 1865; Labor Day honors workers; other days honor the flag and the Constitution.
topics.trouble: Children think every holiday is a day off school about the same thing. Each holiday remembers something different; matching the day to its reason is the skill.

topics.title: Holidays Through the Year
topics.short: Put the national holidays in order through the year, from New Year's Day in January to Christmas Day in December.
topics.trouble: Children order holidays by how much they like them or by the school year (September first). The calendar year starts in January.

topics.title: The First Peoples
topics.short: Native Americans lived across North America for thousands of years before Europeans came, in hundreds of nations with their own languages and ways of life.
topics.trouble: Children think all Native Americans lived the same way, in the same kind of home, or that they lived only long ago. There were (and are) hundreds of different nations.

topics.title: Homes That Fit the Land
topics.short: Native nations built homes from what the land gave them: longhouses of wood and bark, adobe pueblos, tipis on the plains, plank houses by the sea.
topics.trouble: Children think every Native family lived in a tipi. Tipis were homes for peoples who moved across the Great Plains; others built longhouses, pueblos, wigwams or plank houses.

topics.title: Corn, Beans and Squash
topics.short: Many Native farmers grew corn, beans and squash together, the "Three Sisters"; corn and other foods first grown in the Americas are now eaten all over the world.
topics.trouble: Children think Native peoples only hunted. Many nations were skilled farmers; corn, beans, squash, potatoes, tomatoes and pumpkins were first grown in the Americas.

topics.title: Native Nations Today
topics.short: Native nations are still here today, with their own governments, languages and traditions; the federal government recognizes 575 tribes (its January 2026 list).
topics.trouble: Children speak of Native Americans only in the past tense. Native nations live, govern themselves and keep their traditions today.

topics.title: Explorers Cross the Ocean
topics.short: Explorers sailed across the Atlantic Ocean looking for new routes and lands: Leif Erikson about the year 1000, Christopher Columbus in 1492, and many after them.
topics.trouble: Children say Columbus "discovered" an empty land. Millions of people already lived in the Americas; his 1492 voyage began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas.

topics.title: Jamestown, 1607
topics.short: Jamestown, in Virginia, was the first lasting English settlement in America, founded in 1607; the settlers depended on the Powhatan people at first.
topics.trouble: Children think the Pilgrims came first. Jamestown (1607) was settled thirteen years before the Pilgrims landed at Plymouth (1620).

topics.title: The Pilgrims and the Mayflower
topics.short: In 1620 the Pilgrims sailed on the Mayflower to find a place to worship in their own way and founded Plymouth Colony; they agreed to make fair laws together.
topics.trouble: Children think the Pilgrims came to find gold. They came mainly to worship as they believed; the Jamestown settlers had hoped to find riches.

topics.title: The Harvest Feast of 1621
topics.short: Squanto (Tisquantum) and the Wampanoag helped the Pilgrims plant corn, and in 1621 the Pilgrims and about 90 Wampanoag men led by Massasoit shared a three-day harvest feast.
topics.trouble: Children picture a small dinner with turkey and pie. The feast lasted about three days and included deer the Wampanoag brought; we know about it from a letter by a Pilgrim, Edward Winslow.

topics.title: The Thirteen Colonies
topics.short: By 1732 there were thirteen English colonies along the Atlantic coast, from New Hampshire in the north to Georgia in the south.
topics.trouble: Children think the colonies covered the whole country. They were a strip along the Atlantic coast; most of the land west of them was home to Native nations.

topics.title: Why the Colonists Broke Away
topics.short: Britain taxed the colonists, who had no vote in Britain's Parliament; many colonists said that was unfair: "no taxation without representation."
topics.trouble: Children think the colonists simply did not want to pay any taxes. Their complaint was paying taxes that leaders they had not chosen voted on.

topics.title: The Declaration of Independence
topics.short: In 1776 Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence; it says all men are created equal with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
topics.trouble: Children think the Declaration made the colonies free that day. It announced independence; the colonists still had to win the war, which ended in 1783.

topics.title: George Washington
topics.short: George Washington led the Continental Army in the Revolution and became the first President in 1789; he is called the Father of His Country.
topics.trouble: Children think Washington was a king or was President during the whole war. He led the army in the war and was elected President afterward; he chose to step down after two terms.

topics.title: Heroes of the Revolution
topics.short: Many people helped win independence: Paul Revere warned of British soldiers, Ben Franklin won help from France, and soldiers and families of every background served.
topics.trouble: Children think only generals and famous men won the war. Farmers, women who ran farms and shops, Black soldiers and sailors, and allies from France all played a part.

topics.title: The Constitution: Our Country's Rulebook
topics.short: In 1787 leaders wrote the Constitution, the rulebook for our government; it begins "We the People" and still guides the country today.
topics.trouble: Children mix up the Declaration and the Constitution. The Declaration (1776) said we would be free; the Constitution (1787) set up how our government works.

topics.title: Three Branches of Government
topics.short: The Constitution splits the work into three branches: Congress makes the laws, the President carries them out, and the courts decide what the laws mean.
topics.trouble: Children think the President makes all the laws. Congress makes the laws; the President carries them out; the courts settle questions about them.

topics.title: Lewis and Clark
topics.short: In 1804 Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out to explore the West, helped by Sacagawea, a young Shoshone woman, and reached the Pacific Ocean in 1805.
topics.trouble: Children think Lewis and Clark found empty land. They met many Native nations along the way, and Sacagawea and others helped them find routes, food and horses.

topics.title: Pioneers Head West
topics.short: In the 1840s and after, pioneer families traveled west in covered wagons on trails like the Oregon Trail, a trip of about five months.
topics.trouble: Children picture pioneers riding in wagons the whole way. Most walked beside the wagon, which was packed full of food and tools; oxen pulled it.

topics.title: Slavery and Freedom
topics.short: For more than 200 years many Black people in America were enslaved: they were not free and were forced to work without pay; slavery ended in 1865.
topics.trouble: Children think slavery was only in one place or ended when it began to be questioned. It existed in all thirteen colonies, and it took a long struggle and the Civil War to end it.

topics.title: Harriet Tubman and Frederick Douglass
topics.short: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and led others to freedom on the Underground Railroad; Frederick Douglass escaped and became a great speaker and writer against slavery.
topics.trouble: Children think the Underground Railroad was a real train under the ground. It was a secret network of people and hiding places that helped people escape to freedom.

topics.title: Abraham Lincoln
topics.short: Abraham Lincoln, the 16th President, led the country through the Civil War (1861 to 1865), worked to end slavery and kept the country together.
topics.trouble: Children think Lincoln was the first President or lived at the same time as Washington. Lincoln was the 16th President, more than 70 years after Washington.

topics.title: American Inventors
topics.short: Inventors changed how we live: Benjamin Franklin's experiments with electricity, Alexander Graham Bell's telephone (1876), Thomas Edison's light bulb (1879) and the Wright brothers' airplane (1903).
topics.trouble: Children match the invention to the wrong inventor or think inventors worked alone. Edison had a whole team in his laboratory; match each invention to its inventor and its year.

topics.title: Fifty States
topics.short: The country grew from 13 states to 50; the last two, Alaska and Hawaii, became states in 1959, and each state has its own capital city.
topics.trouble: Children think all 50 states joined at once, or that Alaska and Hawaii were the first. States joined one at a time from 1787 to 1959.

topics.title: Clara Barton and Caring for Others
topics.short: Clara Barton cared for wounded soldiers in the Civil War and in 1881 founded the American Red Cross, which still helps people after disasters.
topics.trouble: Children think helpers are only people in uniform today. People have served others throughout history, and many of them were volunteers.

topics.title: Rosa Parks and Dr. King
topics.short: In 1955 Rosa Parks would not give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama; Dr. King helped lead a bus boycott and peaceful marches for equal treatment under the law.
topics.trouble: Children think Rosa Parks was simply tired that day. She said she was tired of giving in; she had worked for fair treatment for years.

topics.title: Footsteps on the Moon
topics.short: On July 20, 1969, American astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon; Armstrong was the first person to walk on it.
topics.trouble: Children think astronauts flew to the Moon in an airplane. They rode a huge rocket, the Saturn V, and landed in a small craft called the Eagle.

topics.title: Then and Now
topics.short: Put the big events of American history in order, from the first peoples to the Moon landing, and compare life long ago with life today.
topics.trouble: Children put Washington, Lincoln and Dr. King all "a long time ago" at the same time. A timeline shows how far apart they were.
